sentences.text: Leptoceratops was approximately 2 meters long and possessed a mix of primitive and derived ceratopsian features.
The largest known individuals of Leptoceratops reached about 2 meters in length and weighed 100 kilograms.
Leptoceratops possesses the largest single-rooted teeth of any ceratopsian, whereas ceratopsids have split, double-rooted teeth.
When first described, the tail neural spines of Leptoceratops were the longest known for any ceratopsian.
The genus Leptoceratops was first described by Barnum Brown in 1914.
Leptoceratops was first discovered in Alberta in 1910 and named in 1914 by Barnum Brown.
Two ceratopsian specimens were discovered in 1910 along the Red Deer River in Alberta by an American Museum of Natural History expedition.
Leptoceratops was first discovered in 1992 in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana by Brig Konecke.
Leptoceratops was a herbivore.
Like other ceratopsians, Leptoceratops was likely a herbivore.
Leptoceratops had an efficient bite capable of processing various food types including angiosperms, conifers, and cycads.
By the time of the Hell Creek Formation, the landscape where Leptoceratops lived was dominated by angiosperms in a forest of small trees.
Leptoceratops was traditionally assumed to be a quadruped.
Leptoceratops had forelimbs long enough to reach the ground upright, enabling a quadrupedal posture.
Leptoceratops was a small dinosaur with short arms and long legs, suggesting it could likely run upright.
Leptoceratops likely moved bipedally at high speeds and quadrupedally when moving slowly.
Leptoceratops had unique teeth among dinosaurs that showed wear patterns driven by a mammal-like jaw rotation during chewing.
A large ridge on the maxilla suggests Leptoceratops had a muscled cheek pouch to help shred large amounts of vegetation.
Leptoceratops teeth exhibit a unique type of tooth-on-tooth wear shared only with Udanoceratops and Archaeoceratops.
Leptoceratops had a unique arcing bite path that created curved wear patterns on its teeth, differing from other neoceratopsians.
Mandibular muscles likely inserted onto the large parietosquamosal frill, giving Leptoceratops a powerful bite.
Fossils from the Hell Creek Formation suggest that Leptoceratops was capable of scratch-digging or burrowing.
In 2019, researchers proposed that Leptoceratops bonebeds represent adults buried during burrow collapses in multi-generational burrows.
Leptoceratops is the namesake genus of the family Leptoceratopsidae.
Leptoceratops was originally classified as a primitive ceratopsian outside the family Ceratopsidae.
Although traditionally linked to Protoceratopsidae, Leptoceratops is now placed in its own family, Leptoceratopsidae, alongside dinosaurs like Udanoceratops and Prenoceratops.
Leptoceratops lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age.
Leptoceratops inhabited a semi-humid floodplain environment with braided streams and small-treed forests.
Fossil material of Leptoceratops was found 75 meters below the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary in the middle Hell Creek Formation.
It is debated whether Leptoceratops is unrelated to other forms, belongs within Protoceratopsidae, or forms a clade with genera like Montanoceratops and Udanoceratops.
It is debated whether Leptoceratops was as ecologically restricted to cool environments as previously thought, given its presence in coastal plain formations.
While most studies suggest Leptoceratops is outside Protoceratopsidae and Ceratopsidae, some studies suggest it may be allied with Ceratopsidae.
